theme: The plot; the anointing; the Last Supper; Gethsemane
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 26:1-46. The plot against Jesus, the anointing at Bethany, Judas’s betrayal, the Last Supper, Peter’s denial predicted, and Gethsemane. Read the words of institution (26:26-29) and the prayer in the garden (26:36-46) slowly.
settingTheScene: It is Passover week. The religious leaders are plotting to arrest Jesus quietly. At the same time, a woman anoints him with costly perfume, Judas bargains to betray him, and Jesus shares the Passover meal with his disciples. In the garden afterward, he prays in anguish. Matthew shows that everything is happening according to the Scriptures, and that Jesus goes to the cross willingly.
observation: “You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified” (26:2).
“Why this waste? For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor” (26:8-9).
“What will you give me if I deliver him to you?” (26:15).
“For this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (26:28).
“Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (26:35).
“My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me” (26:38).
“My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (26:39).
interpretation:
The chapter moves between devotion and betrayal. A woman pours an expensive jar of ointment on Jesus’ head, and the disciples object to the waste. Jesus defends her: she has prepared him for burial, and her act will be remembered. Immediately afterward, Judas goes to the chief priests and sells Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. The price recalls Zechariah 11:12, the price of a slave.

At the Passover meal, Jesus predicts that one of them will betray him. Each asks, “Is it I, Lord?” Then he takes bread and wine and gives them new meaning. The bread is his body and the cup is his blood of the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins. This is the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31. The Passover lamb saved Israel from judgment, and Jesus is the Lamb whose blood saves his people. He also promises that he will drink it new with them in the Father’s kingdom.

On the way to the Mount of Olives, he tells the disciples that they will all fall away. Peter protests that he will never deny him. Jesus says that before the rooster crows, he will deny him three times.

In Gethsemane, we see Jesus in anguish. “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.” He falls on his face and prays, “Let this cup pass from me.” The cup is the cup of God’s wrath against sin. Yet he adds, “Not as I will, but as you will.” The second Adam, in a garden, submits to the Father’s will where the first Adam rebelled. He prays three times, and the disciples sleep. Then he stands: “Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.”
connection: Exodus 12 describes the first Passover. Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises the new covenant. Zechariah 11:12-13 and 13:7 are fulfilled in the thirty pieces and the scattering of the sheep. Isaiah 51:17 describes the cup of the LORD’s wrath. Hebrews 5:7-8 describes Jesus’ prayers with loud cries and tears. 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 gives Paul’s account of the Lord’s Supper. Genesis 3 and Romans 5:19 contrast Adam’s disobedience with Christ’s obedience. Luke 22:44.
application:
If you are able, take the Lord’s Supper this week, and think about what “the forgiveness of sins” cost him.

In your own Gethsemane, whatever that may be, pray as Jesus did: “Not as I will, but as you will.”

Ask where you have said, “I will never deny you,” and been overconfident.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for the bread and cup given for the forgiveness of your sins.
Ask him to keep you awake and praying when you are tempted to sleep.
Tell him what cup you are afraid to drink, and pray, “Not my will but yours.”
